title: ASME Stamp Audit NDE Support in Birmingham, AL
description: ASME stamp audit help for Birmingham fabricators: NDE written practice, procedures, records and lab control, reviewed by a Level III. Request a gap review.
h1: ASME Certification Audit Support in Birmingham, Alabama: The NDE Side of Your Joint Review
html:
This page is for Birmingham-area fabricators and repair shops working toward a new ASME Certificate of Authorization, or getting ready to renew one, who want the nondestructive examination part of their quality control system to hold up at the joint review. Atlantis NDT is an ASNT NDT Level III consulting company: we review or draft the NDE written practice, procedures, personnel records and subcontractor controls, then take your people through a mock review before the real team arrives. To talk through your certificate scope, send us a short note. We reply within one business day.

Birmingham fabrication and the step into Code work

Birmingham grew up on iron, steel and pipe, and the metro still has a deep bench of steel fabricators, machine shops, foundries and mill-maintenance contractors. Many of those shops learned their trade on structural steel, crane runways and mill repair, where AWS D1.1 and the customer's drawings set the rules. The move into ASME work usually starts with a customer request. A utility wants a replacement header or a set of air receivers. A pulp and paper mill needs a heat exchanger shell, a blow tank or a digester repair. A chemical plant on one of Alabama's rivers wants process vessels from a supplier it can drive to. The shop applies for a U, S or PP designator, or for a National Board R certificate to make repairs, and the NDE that used to mean "the inspector checks the welds" now has to live inside a written quality control system that an Authorized Inspector reviews.

The local work mix is unusually broad. Alabama runs a large power-generation fleet, a long list of pulp and paper mills, and chemical, metals and pipe plants spread from the Tennessee Valley down to the Mobile corridor. A Birmingham shop can see Section I boiler parts, Section VIII vessels and B31.1 or B31.3 piping in the same year, and steel-industry customers add heavy plate and thick sections. That mix pushes the NDE program toward magnetic particle testing on carbon steel, ultrasonic examination of thick welds and plate, and radiography that is almost always bought from a licensed outside company.

How Alabama regulates boilers and pressure vessels

Boilers and pressure vessels in Alabama come under the Alabama Boiler and Pressure Vessel Safety Act (Act No. 2000-315). The Inspections section of the Alabama Department of Workforce administers it under a state chief inspector; older documents and some National Board listings still name the former Department of Labor, so do not be thrown by the two names. The working rules sit in chapter 480-7 of the Alabama Administrative Code, and several of them reach straight into a stamp shop:

  • Current editions by default. The rules adopt the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, the National Board Inspection Code and related standards in their most current editions unless the Boiler Board says otherwise. Your shop cannot plan on Alabama lagging a few editions behind.
  • "Standard" objects. The rules describe a standard boiler or vessel as one that bears the ASME stamp and a National Board number, and an installation request for such an object includes the Manufacturer's Data Report. Your NDE results are summarized on that report, so the report and the examination records must agree.
  • Permits and certificates. Installing a boiler or pressure vessel needs a permit, and regulated equipment must carry a current operating certificate. Pressure vessels receive a certificate inspection every two years and power boilers every year.
  • Repairs and alterations. Rule 480-7-5-.06 sends repairs to the latest NBIC (or to the API pressure vessel inspection code where that code applies), requires NBIC work to be done by a valid National Board R certificate holder whose authorization covers the job, makes the work subject to acceptance by the in-service inspector, and requires the documentation to reach the chief inspector.
  • Owner-user inspection. Companies with an established inspection department can be recognized as owner-user inspection agencies. Large mills and chemical sites often are, and their inspectors become part of your audience whenever you repair their equipment.

The practical effect is that the paper trail from your shop reaches the state. If the radiography report on a repaired nozzle does not match the R form, the inspector responsible for that vessel in service will notice. Before your review, confirm the edition in force and any recent rule changes with the chief inspector's office.

From structural habits to an ASME NDE system

Shops coming off AWS D1.1 work often expect their existing NDE setup to carry over. Some of it does. D1.1 already expects NDT personnel to be qualified under SNT-TC-1A or CP-189, so a shop with a certified Level II magnetic particle technician and a written practice is not starting from nothing. The differences sit in four places.

  • Procedures. ASME work is examined to written procedures that meet ASME Section V: Article 7 for magnetic particle, Article 4 for ultrasonic examination of welds, Article 2 for radiography and so on. A D1.1 ultrasonic procedure built around that code's decibel indication rating does not satisfy Article 4, which calibrates to reference reflectors and hands evaluation to the acceptance rules of the construction code.
  • Acceptance criteria. Pass and fail come from the book section. Under Section VIII Division 1 that means the full and spot radiography rules in UW-51 and UW-52, the rounded-indication charts in Appendix 4, and the magnetic particle, penetrant and ultrasonic appendices. Each technique sheet should name the paragraph it is judged against.
  • The Authorized Inspector. On structural jobs the owner's inspector may never look at your NDE paperwork. Under a stamp, the Authorized Inspector sets hold points, can ask to witness a procedure demonstration where Section V calls for one, and reviews examination records before signing the data report.
  • The QC manual. Every NDE control has to be written into the manual and then carried out the way the manual says. A practice that works but is not written down is a finding.

A useful test before you apply: take one recent structural job and read it as an Authorized Inspector would. Who examined the welds, to which procedure, under which certification, with which calibrated yoke or flaw detector, and where is the report filed? The gaps that exercise exposes are the gaps a review team finds.

Where NDE usually sits in a Birmingham stamp shop

Most small and mid-size Code shops in the metro run a split arrangement. The welding inspector or quality manager does visual examination in house. One or two employees certified to Level II under the shop's own written practice handle magnetic particle and liquid penetrant work. Radiography, and most ultrasonic examination of welds, is bought from commercial NDE companies, because radiography needs a radioactive materials license, a radiation safety program and qualified radiographers that a fabricator rarely wants to carry. Radiography is outside what Atlantis does in the United States; when RT is in your scope, a licensed contractor makes the exposures, and a Level III can review the radiographs and the technique on your behalf.

The split arrangement works, but it raises three questions the team will ask:

  1. How does the QC manual qualify and accept the outside company's written practice, personnel certifications and procedures? ASME's joint review guidance says that when NDE is bought in, the team expects to see the subcontractor's procedure and personnel qualification files at the place where the review happens. A lab that keeps them in its own office does not meet that.
  2. Who in your company reviews the subcontractor's reports and radiographs before they go to the Authorized Inspector, and what qualifies that person to do it?
  3. How do you control in-house MT and PT: written practice, examinations, annual vision checks, yoke lift tests, light-meter checks and consumable batch records?

On the in-house side, the Division 1 appendices for magnetic particle and penetrant work describe their own route for the manufacturer to certify examiner competence and vision, while many shops simply keep those examiners under the same SNT-TC-1A written practice they require of the outside lab. Either route can be defended. What fails is a manual that names one route while the training files follow the other.

What the joint review team will examine

Think of the joint review as a manual check followed by a shop visit. Before arriving, the team reads your quality control manual. On site there is an opening meeting and a plant walk, then the long middle stretch ASME calls implementation, then a private team discussion, then an exit meeting where you hear the results. The team works under a team leader with your Authorized Inspection Agency, and ASME makes the final decision on the certificate. During implementation you demonstrate the program on actual Code work, on a mock-up that will not be stamped, or both. The demonstration has to suit each designator requested; a Section VIII Division 1 item covers U, S and PP among others, but a U2 request needs a Division 2 design package.

On the NDE side, expect the team to follow the demonstration item through your system. The drawing called for a spot or full examination; a qualified person examined the joint to a written procedure; the result was judged against the right acceptance paragraph; the Authorized Inspector saw the record; the result reached the data report. At renewal you list all Code work done since the last review, in the shop and at field sites, and any NDE record behind that list can be pulled.

Findings we see most often in shops with Birmingham's profile:

  • The written practice cites an older SNT-TC-1A edition than the one the QC manual names.
  • A Level II magnetic particle examiner's annual vision record is missing, or was signed by someone the practice does not authorize.
  • The outside lab's procedures were never formally reviewed and accepted against Section V.
  • Ultrasonic technique sheets omit the calibration block, the scanning sensitivity or the acceptance reference.
  • Yoke lift tests and black-light intensity checks were done but never recorded.
  • Spot radiograph locations cannot be traced to the welder whose work they represent.

Repair shops and the R certificate in Alabama

A good share of Birmingham's Code work is repair: boiler tube and header work at mills and power stations, nozzle and shell repairs on process vessels, and alterations when a plant re-rates equipment. That work runs under the National Board Inspection Code, and the NDE has to satisfy the original code of construction, not whatever the repair crew is used to. Alabama's rule that NBIC repairs be done by an R holder, accepted by the in-service inspector and documented to the chief inspector means a weak NDE record shows up twice: once to the plant's inspector and once at the state. Our NBIC R-stamp NDE audit support page covers the R review itself; the national guide to ASME audit Level III support sets out the full scope for new-construction certificates.

What Atlantis does for Birmingham shops, on site and remotely

Site work in Alabama means a trip from Atlantis's Houston office, while most document work is handled remotely. A typical scope:

  • Written practice. Review or write the NDE written practice to the SNT-TC-1A or CP-189 edition your Code edition calls for, covering in-house methods and the rules for accepting outside personnel.
  • Procedures and technique sheets. Draft or review MT, PT, VT and UT procedures against Section V, plus the radiographic technique requirements your shop places on its outside lab, through our procedure development service.
  • Demonstrations. Prepare the procedure demonstration an Authorized Inspector may ask to witness, as set out on our procedure qualification and demonstration page.
  • Personnel records. Audit training hours, experience, examination results and vision records, and administer Level II examinations under your written practice when you need a Level III to give them. Your company still signs each certification.
  • Subcontractor control. Build the acceptance file for each NDE lab and the manual wording behind it, using the method on our subcontractor approval audits page.
  • Mock review and findings. Run a mock implementation on your demonstration item, write up the gaps, and help you close findings from the real review with corrective-action evidence.

The founder, Anoop Rayavarapu, leads Birmingham engagements himself; his ASNT NDT Level III covers MT, UT, VT, PT and RT, the methods a metals-country shop leans on, and he has more than 11 years of field work behind him. If your in-house examiners need method training before certification, see NDT training for Birmingham; for examinations at your site, our ultrasonic testing in Birmingham page explains how UT crews are scoped.

What stays with your company, your inspector and your welding engineer

Clear lines save time in front of the team. Your company owns its quality control system and its certificate, and your quality manager answers the team. Your company certifies its NDE personnel under its written practice; Atlantis can examine, review and recommend, but the signature is yours. The Authorized Inspector and the review team decide whether the system is acceptable. Atlantis is not an Authorized Inspection Agency, not an ASME reviewer and not a certification body.

Your welding program, meaning WPS, PQR and welder qualifications under ASME Section IX, belongs to your welding engineer or quality manager; Atlantis does not write or qualify welding procedures. Our WPS, PQR and WPQ guide explains what that program covers. Nuclear certificates are outside our scope: Atlantis does not support Section III, N-type certificates or NQA-1 programs.

Birmingham audit-readiness checklist

  • QC manual, written practice and procedures all cite the same SNT-TC-1A or CP-189 edition, and that edition is the one your Code edition accepts.
  • Each in-house examiner has a certification file with training hours, experience, examination results, a current vision record and the signature of the person the practice authorizes.
  • Every D1.1-only procedure is either retired or clearly labelled as not for Code work, so nobody pulls the wrong one on a stamped job.
  • Each outside NDE company has an acceptance file in your shop: its written practice, current certifications for the people it sends, its procedures with your review recorded, and evidence of equipment calibration.
  • Copies of those subcontractor records will be at your facility on review day, not only at the lab.
  • Yokes, flaw detectors, thickness gauges, light meters and reference blocks are on a calibration list with due dates, and nothing past due sits on the shop floor.
  • Penetrant and magnetic particle consumables have batch records you can tie to the examinations that used them.
  • Your NDE report forms carry the information the Data Report and the Authorized Inspector need: joint, procedure, examiner, technique, result and acceptance reference.
  • Spot radiograph and UT locations trace to welders, so a rejected spot triggers the additional examinations the Code requires.
  • For repair work, your R-form package shows the NDE performed to the original code of construction.
  • Your demonstration item, or the live job you will use, actually exercises the NDE methods in your scope.
  • The person who will answer NDE questions on review day has walked through the file at least once with someone playing the reviewer.

Records that live in spreadsheets tend to fail the expiry and calibration items first; our pages on expired technician certifications and equipment past calibration show how a shop keeps those dates in front of people.

How an engagement runs

  1. Scoping call. We confirm the designators you hold or want, your review date, your Authorized Inspection Agency, and which methods are in house versus subcontracted.
  2. Document pull. You send the QC manual NDE sections, written practice, procedures, a sample of personnel files and your subcontractor files.
  3. Gap report. We return a written list of gaps ranked by what a review team is likely to write up, with the Code or practice reference for each.
  4. Drafting and correction. We draft or revise documents for your approval; your quality manager decides what goes into the manual.
  5. Site visit. We travel to Birmingham for a mock implementation on your demonstration item, a records walkthrough with your team, and any Level III examinations you need given.
  6. Review support and close-out. We stay available to your quality manager around the review and help assemble corrective-action evidence if the team leaves findings.

What to send us to start: the NDE sections of your QC manual, your written practice, the procedure list, two or three personnel certification files, the acceptance file for each NDE subcontractor, your calibration list and one completed job package with its Data Report. The NDT audit consulting page explains our general audit method if you want it before calling.

faq.q: Do we need our own Level III to get an ASME U stamp?
faq.a: Not necessarily. SNT-TC-1A lets an employer use an outside agency for Level III functions, provided the written practice says so and names who performs them. Atlantis can act as that outside Level III for UT, RT, MT, PT and VT examinations and procedure approval, while your company keeps the authority to certify its own people. See our Level III consulting page.

faq.q: Can our structural CWI do visual examination on Code work?
faq.a: A CWI certificate shows welding inspection competence, but it is not by itself a certification under your NDE written practice. Your QC manual has to state how visual examiners are qualified for Code work, and the records must match. Many Birmingham shops add VT to the written practice and certify the CWI under it.

faq.q: Our radiography is subcontracted. What will the review team want to see?
faq.a: The lab's written practice, current certifications for its radiographers and interpreters, its procedures with your acceptance recorded, and the radiographs and reports for Code jobs. ASME's guidance expects those files to be on hand where the review takes place, so keep copies in your shop.

faq.q: Does Alabama require National Board registration for new vessels?
faq.a: Alabama's rules describe a standard boiler or pressure vessel as one bearing the ASME stamp and a National Board number, and installation requests for those objects include the Manufacturer's Data Report. Confirm what your customer's installation will need with the chief inspector's office at the Alabama Department of Workforce.

No. Atlantis holds no industrial radiography license in the US and does not shoot film or digital images here. A licensed radiography company makes the exposures; Atlantis can review radiographs, radiographic procedures and technique details as a Level III, and can help you set the requirements your shop places on the lab.

faq.q: Which SNT-TC-1A edition should our written practice follow?
faq.a: The edition your construction code and Section V Article 1 accept for the Code edition you build to, and the same edition everywhere in your manual. Mismatched editions between the manual and the practice are one of the most common NDE findings.

faq.q: How much of the preparation can be done remotely?
faq.a: Most of it. Document review, drafting, gap reports and personnel file audits are remote. A site visit to Birmingham is worth it for the mock implementation, procedure demonstration practice and any Level III examinations you want given in person.

faq.q: Will Atlantis help with our WPS and PQR files?
faq.a: No. The welding program belongs to your welding engineer or quality manager, and Atlantis does not write or qualify welding procedures. Our WPS, PQR and WPQ guide explains what reviewers expect from that program.

faq.q: What if the review team leaves NDE findings?
faq.a: We help you find the cause, correct the documents or records, and assemble corrective-action evidence for the team or your Authorized Inspection Agency. The decision on the certificate stays with ASME.

faq.q: Do you support N-type certificates for nuclear work?
faq.a: No. Section III, N-type certificates and NQA-1 programs are outside Atlantis's scope. We support non-nuclear certificates such as U, S, PP and the National Board R certificate.
